unit: MAE of log10(DFT-calculated poly_total dielectric constant); 0.12 log10 is about a factor of 1.32
tuned_trees_config: GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=600, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.03, subsample=0.8, random_state=42), the winner of 8 configs on 3-fold GroupKFold over training rows only (CV MAE 0.1216). Fixed 300/4/0.05 scored CV 0.1246.
leaks: None found. (a) Input and target standardisation in fitNet uses only the rows passed to it (training rows, or the fold's training rows in CV). Each feature is computed from its own row, log10 is applied per row, and there is no clipping or global statistic.

(b) Train and test share 0 group ids. I re-parsed the raw formulas myself and found 0 test rows whose reduced formula appears in training, 0 duplicate material_ids, 0 test rows with an input vector identical to a training row, and 0 test rows whose 31 composition features match a training row.

(c) The settings (6-config grid), the choice of 5 members (ensemble CV vs single CV) and the epoch count all came from 3-fold grouped CV on training rows only. The folds are disjoint by group and cover all 843 rows. Epochs are fixed at 150 with no early stopping, and no ensemble member is dropped. The test split was read only to score the final model.

(d) The 42 inputs contain no n, poly_electronic, pot_ferroelectric, e_electronic, e_total or band_gap. The largest absolute correlation between any feature and these columns is n 0.46, poly_electronic 0.26 and band_gap 0.52, so no feature copies them. band_gap appears only in the separately labelled second model.

(e) The Mlp class matches /workspace/ncsu-hackathon/src/lib/nn.js exactly. Weights start from seeded random He initialisation, and prediction is only the average forward pass of 5 networks: no trees, no nearest-neighbour or table lookup of training labels, no pre-trained weights.

Minor caveat the report already states: the network settings were chosen on seed-42 training rows, which overlap the test rows of the 8 extra splits, so the 8-split comparison leans slightly toward the network. This does not affect the single-split numbers above.
safe_sentence: Our small neural network, written from scratch in JavaScript, estimates a compound's DFT-calculated dielectric constant from its formula, symmetry and cell volume with a typical error of about a factor of 1.3 (0.121 log10 on 213 held-out compounds, against 0.213 for always guessing the average). Standard gradient-boosted trees do as well or slightly better (0.112 to 0.117), and both badly underestimate the rare high-dielectric compounds.
unsafe_sentence: Do not say: "Our neural network beats standard machine learning and accurately predicts measured dielectric constants, including high-k materials." The trees beat it, the targets are calculated rather than measured, and it misses values above 30 by about a factor of 2.
verdict: The numbers reproduce exactly and I found no leak. I retrained their 5-member, 64-32 Huber network with their trainer and settings (8.6 s) and got test MAE 0.1211 log10, which matches the claim and their saved test predictions to within 0.0. With my own scoring, the naive training mean gets 0.2131 and their fixed trees get 0.1173, both as claimed. When I tuned the trees modestly with grouped CV on training rows only (winner: 600 trees, depth 6, learning rate 0.03), they scored 0.1116 on test, better than the network by about 0.0095 log10 (paired bootstrap 95% interval [-0.002, +0.021], so the gap is borderline, not decisive). The network clearly beats the naive guess but does not beat fixed or tuned trees. The report already says this honestly ('statistically indistinguishable', 'not better than the trees'), so the team must not present the network as the winner. All targets are DFT calculations, not measurements, and the cell volume input is itself a DFT relaxed-cell output.
